title: The algorithm tour
html:
Purpose. Linear and logistic regression are two of many algorithms. You do not need to master all of them now, but you should know what each one is for, what it is good and bad at, and which one to try first. This chapter is the tour, based on Infinite Codes' 17-minute overview and extended with practical advice.

Key ideas

  • Almost every algorithm is either supervised (learn from labels) or unsupervised (find structure).
  • For tables of data, the usual strong choices are random forests and gradient boosting. Start with a simple baseline, then compare.
  • Some algorithms need scaled features (nearest neighbours, SVM, neural networks, k-means, PCA); trees do not.
  • Choose by measuring on held-out data (Chapter 12), not by reputation.

13.1 Supervised algorithms

K-nearest neighbours (KNN). To predict for a new case, find the K most similar cases in the training data and take the majority vote (classification) or the average (regression). Analogy: ask the five people who live closest to you which restaurant is good. There is no training step at all: the data is the model. K is a hyperparameter. A small K overfits, because one odd neighbour decides, and a large K underfits. It needs scaled features, because distance mixes them, and it is slow on big data. Loan: judge a new application like its 5 most similar past ones.

Support vector machine (SVM). Draws the boundary between two classes with the widest possible empty margin, like the widest street you can fit between two neighbourhoods. A trick called a kernel lets the street curve. It works well on medium-sized data and needs scaled features. Loan: approve or decline from income and debt. The video's own example separates cats from elephants by weight and nose length.

Naive Bayes. Uses Bayes' theorem (Chapter 15) and naively assumes that features are independent given the class, so it just multiplies simple probabilities. The assumption is wrong, but it is fast and works surprisingly well for text. Its probabilities are often poorly calibrated. Loan: sort customer emails into complaints and questions. The classic example is the spam filter.

Decision tree. A chain of yes or no questions ("credit score below 650? amount above 20,000?"), chosen so that each final leaf is as pure as possible, meaning mostly one class. Analogy: the game of twenty questions. It is easy to explain and needs no scaling, but a deep tree memorizes the data (overfits) and changes a lot when the data changes a little. Loan: "credit score below X? amount above Y?" The video's example is heart-attack risk.

Random forest. Many trees, each trained on a random sample of the rows and a random subset of the features, then a vote. Analogy: a hundred doctors, each given a differently redacted copy of the patient file, who vote. Each doctor is unreliable alone, but their mistakes differ, so the vote is steady. This is bagging, and it mainly cuts variance (Chapter 11). Hard to overfit, little tuning, less interpretable than one tree.

Boosting (AdaBoost, gradient boosting, XGBoost and relatives). Trees built one after another, each trying to fix the errors of the previous ones. Analogy: a tutor who sets the next lesson only on the questions you got wrong. It is often the most accurate method on tables of data, but it overfits more easily than a random forest and trains more slowly. Key settings: the number of trees, their depth and the learning rate. Loan: the classic tool for default prediction.

Neural networks. Layers of simple units that learn their own features. Chapter 14. The video's example is recognizing handwritten digits.

13.2 Unsupervised algorithms

K-means (clustering). Pick K centres, assign every point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its points, and repeat until nothing changes. Analogy: choose where to put K pizza shops so that everyone has a shop nearby, then move each shop to the middle of its own customers. You must choose K (often by trying several and looking for the bend in the error curve), the features must be scaled, and it assumes roundish groups. Loan: customer segments. The video's example is emails grouped into three unnamed groups.

Hierarchical clustering and DBSCAN. Hierarchical clustering repeatedly merges the two closest groups and gives a tree of merges (a dendrogram) from which you cut at the level you like. DBSCAN finds dense regions, can find groups of any shape, and labels isolated points as noise, which also makes it useful for spotting oddities.

PCA (principal component analysis). Rotates the axes to point along the directions of greatest variation, then keeps only the first few. Analogy: the shadow of a 3D object on a wall, from the angle that keeps the most of its shape. Use it to compress many correlated columns, to draw high-dimensional data in 2D, or to remove redundancy. The new columns are mixtures of the old ones, so they are harder to interpret. Loan: thirty related financial ratios become five components. The video's example: fish length and height become one "shape" feature.

13.3 A comparison, in one table

Algorithm Family Needs scaling Strength Watch out for scikit-learn class
Logistic regression supervised, classification yes fast, explainable, a strong baseline only straight boundaries unless you add features LogisticRegression
KNN supervised, both yes no training, simple idea slow on big data, sensitive to K KNeighborsClassifier
SVM supervised, mostly classification yes good on medium data, curved boundaries slow on big data, tuning SVC
Naive Bayes supervised, classification no very fast, good for text wrong independence assumption GaussianNB, MultinomialNB
Decision tree supervised, both no explainable, handles mixed data overfits, unstable DecisionTreeClassifier
Random forest supervised, ensemble no strong, robust, little tuning less explainable, bigger RandomForestClassifier
Gradient boosting / XGBoost supervised, ensemble no often the best on tables overfits, needs tuning GradientBoostingClassifier
K-means unsupervised, clustering yes simple, fast you choose K, round groups KMeans
PCA unsupervised, dimensionality reduction yes compression, visualization components are hard to read PCA

13.4 Try them, then measure

In scikit-learn every supervised model has the same interface, so comparing them takes a loop and cross-validation (Chapter 12). This is a synthetic dataset with 8 features, 4 of them informative, and the scores are the average accuracy over five folds:

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=600, n_features=8, n_informative=4, random_state=0)
models = {
    "logistic regression": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()),
    "k-nearest neighbours": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)),
    "support vector machine": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC()),
    "naive Bayes": GaussianNB(),
    "decision tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0),
    "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0),
    "gradient boosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
}
for name, model in models.items():
    print(f"{name:<24} {cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")
Model Accuracy
logistic regression 0.698
k-nearest neighbours 0.938
support vector machine 0.937
naive Bayes 0.712
decision tree 0.910
random forest 0.955
gradient boosting 0.953

Here the data has curved structure, so the straight-boundary models (logistic regression, naive Bayes) fall far behind, and the forest and boosting lead. On a different dataset the order will differ, which is exactly why you measure instead of assuming. The sensible routine on a table of data: build the simple baseline first, then try a random forest and gradient boosting, compare with cross-validation, and keep the simpler model if the difference is within the spread of the scores.

Two unsupervised sketches on made-up data: K-means with K = 3 on three blobs of 100 points returns groups of 100, 101 and 99 points. PCA on two strongly related columns (a fish's length and height) puts 98.8% of the variation into its first component, so one column nearly replaces two.

Common mistakes

  • Using nearest neighbours, SVM or k-means on unscaled features.
  • Picking a favourite algorithm instead of comparing on held-out data.
  • Choosing K for k-means by eye, then explaining the clusters as if they were facts.
  • Reaching for a neural network on a small table, where a forest or logistic regression usually wins.

Check yourself

  • Which algorithms in this chapter need feature scaling, and why?
  • Why does a random forest overfit less than one deep decision tree?
  • What is the difference between clustering and classification?
  • You have 3,000 loans and 20 columns. Which two models do you try first, and how do you pick?
Show answers

(1) KNN, SVM, neural networks, k-means and PCA, because they use distances or sums over features, so a feature measured in thousands would dominate. (2) Many different trees vote, and their individual errors partly cancel (lower variance). (3) Classification has known labels and learns them; clustering has none and invents groups. (4) A regularized logistic regression as the baseline and a random forest or gradient boosting, compared with cross-validation on a held-out set.
